title: Mapping Data to Components
summary: Replaces three hand-written Card components with one Array.prototype.map() call that turns each object in contacts.js into a <Card/>. Introduces React's required, unique key prop for list items, and a mini debugging challenge showing that key is never passed through to props.

concepts.heading: Why map components
points: Hard-coding <Card name={contacts[0].name} .../>, <Card name={contacts[1].name} .../> and so on is repetitive and only works for a fixed number of items.
Mapping generates one component per array element, so the UI follows the data automatically: add an object to the array (e.g. later from a form) and a new card appears with no JSX changes.
contacts.js holds an array of objects that all share the same shape (id, name, imgURL, phone, email) but with different values. That uniform shape is what makes a single template function possible.

concepts.heading: Calling map() inside JSX
points: Comment out the three hard-coded cards in App.jsx and write contacts.map(...) in their place, inside the wrapper div.
Inside JSX children, bare text is rendered literally, so contacts.map() must be wrapped in curly braces: {contacts.map(createCard)}. The braces switch JSX into JavaScript-expression mode.
map() takes a function as its argument (a callback). Passing a function into a function is a core idea of functional programming, and it can be nested many levels deep.
Pass the function by name with no parentheses: contacts.map(createCard). Writing createCard() would call it once immediately instead of handing it to map.
map() loops over the array, calls the callback once per element with that single element (one contact object, not the whole array) as its argument, and collects every return value into a new array.
React can render an array of elements directly, so the array of <Card/> elements returned by map() appears as a list of cards.

concepts.heading: The createCard callback
points: Define function createCard(contact) above App. Its parameter is one contact object on each call.
It returns a <Card/> whose props are filled from that object: name={contact.name}, img={contact.imgURL}, tel={contact.phone}, email={contact.email}.

The prop names (name, img, tel, email) must match what the Card component reads from props; the object property names (imgURL, phone) come from contacts.js. The two sets of names do not have to be the same.
React DevTools (Components tab) confirms each Card now receives the expected props.

concepts.heading: The key prop
points: After mapping, the console warns that each child in a list needs a unique key. Refreshing does not clear it, so it is a genuine React warning rather than a sandbox glitch.
React keeps a virtual DOM of the page; when components are produced in a loop it needs a stable identity for each one so it can update, reorder and re-render list items efficiently.
Fix: add key={contact.id} to the returned <Card/>. The ids in contacts.js (1, 2, 3) are unique, so they make good keys.
Rules: the prop must be spelled exactly key (lowercase); its value may be a string or a number; it must be unique among the sibling components generated by that loop.

(Extra) Keys only need to be unique among siblings, not across the whole app. Using the array index as a key is a fallback that causes bugs when items are reordered, inserted or deleted, so prefer a real id from the data.

(Extra) During re-rendering React compares the old and new list element by element using the keys: a matching key means 'same item, update it', a new key means 'create', a missing key means 'remove'. This is why keys must be stable and unique.

concepts.heading: Debugging challenge: key is not readable inside the component
points:

Trying {props.key} renders nothing and triggers a console warning saying key is not a prop and reading it gives undefined.
React DevTools shows why: the Card's props list contains name, img, tel and email but no key. React consumes key internally to order and track the list and strips it from props.

Solution: pass the same value again under a normal prop name, e.g. id={contact.id}, alongside key={contact.id}, then render {props.id} inside Card. It looks duplicated, but key is reserved for React and id is for your own use.
Takeaway: get used to React DevTools and console warnings for debugging; bugs are normal, and the tools show what props a component actually received.

pitfalls: Writing contacts.map(createCard) without curly braces inside JSX, which prints it as text.
Calling the callback (map(createCard())) instead of passing it.
Forgetting key, or using a value that repeats across items, which keeps the 'unique key' warning.
Misspelling key (Key, keys) so React does not recognise it.
Expecting props.key to work inside the child component; it is always undefined.
Mixing up prop names and data property names (img vs imgURL, tel vs phone).

(Extra) Reference repo divergence: the student's contacts.js has no id fields, so key={contact.id} and id={contact.id} are undefined there and the key warning would remain; add id: 1, 2, 3 to each object. The repo also renames Card to ContactCard, uses props imgURL/phone instead of img/tel, uses a named export (export {contacts} with import { contacts } from "./contacts.js") instead of a default export, and keeps App.jsx in src (so the path is ./contacts.js rather than ../contacts).

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'Mapping data to components' (s36). Blurb: turn an array of objects into a list of React components with map(), and learn why React needs a unique key on each one.
Task 1: replace three hard-coded <Card/> elements with {contacts.map(createCard)}.
Task 2: write createCard(contact) that returns a Card with name, img, tel and email props filled from the object.
Task 3: add key={contact.id} and make the console warning disappear.
Task 4: show the id on each card, which forces the learner to discover that props.key is undefined and pass id separately.
Starter code: contacts.js with 3 objects (id, name, imgURL, phone, email), a working Card/Avatar/Detail set, and App.jsx with the repetitive hard-coded cards.

Interactive demo: an editable contacts array on the left and live cards on the right; an 'Add contact' button pushes a new object and a card appears. Include a toggle that removes keys (or uses index keys) and shows the console warning plus a reorder button that reveals stale state with index keys.
Explore panel: a props inspector for each card showing that key is absent from props while id is present.
